title: Modelling missing modalities in multi-omics clinical outcome prediction
abstract: Abstract Multi-omics integration has become central to precision medicine, yet in real-world clinical cohorts, complete multi-layer profiling is rarely achieved. Cost, assay failure, and evolving study design frequently produce block-wise modality missingness, where entire omics layers are absent for subsets of patients. This setting poses a distinct challenge for predictive modelling and biomarker discovery, as conventional integrative methods often assume fully paired data or rely on complete-case filtering or point-wise imputation, leading to information loss or biased inference. In response, a growing class of methods has been developed to learn from partially observed multi-omics data through missingness-aware fusion, shared latent representations with subset-conditioned inference, and modality-completion frameworks. This review presents a methodological taxonomy of approaches designed to support outcome modelling under heterogeneous modality availability, with a primary focus on patient-level bulk data and clinical prediction tasks, while also discussing representation-learning frameworks developed for single-cell or unsupervised settings where the missing-modality handling mechanism is architecturally transferable to supervised clinical prediction. We contrast design philosophies, inference mechanisms, and robustness properties, and examine when strategies developed for single-cell mosaic integration transfer to cohort-level modelling. By clarifying the assumptions, robustness properties, and empirical behaviour of missing-modality strategies, we aim to provide a principled framework for selecting and developing models suited to partially observed multi-omics datasets in real-world clinical contexts.

title: Translating deep learning innovations into clinical medical imaging practice
abstract: Deep learning (DL) has fundamentally transformed medical imaging, enabling unprecedented advancements in image quality, automated detection, and diagnostic precision. Despite these technical achievements, a significant translational gap persists between algorithmic development and robust clinical deployment. Unlike prior reviews that focus primarily on algorithmic architectures or single modalities, this structured narrative review provides a comprehensive translational roadmap bridging technical methodologies with clinical applications and market dynamics. We synthesize recent findings across multiple imaging modalities, including X-ray, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound, positron emission tomography (PET), and digital pathology, and uniquely integrate seven application domains, including image classification, segmentation, object tracking, augmented imaging, disease prediction, computer-aided diagnosis (CAD), and radiomics, and examine the emerging role of foundation models and vision-language models that are reshaping the paradigm from task-specific to generalizable medical AI. To evaluate market translation, we analyze the expansive landscape of over 1300 FDA-cleared AI/machine learning (ML)-enabled medical devices and compare evolving international frameworks governing clinical deployment, specifically the FDA, EMA, and the EU AI Act. Our analysis reveals that while DL achieves specialist-level performance, cleared devices predominantly focus on radiology triage rather than autonomous diagnosis, and widespread adoption remains hindered by data quality challenges, limited model interpretability, and complex regulatory requirements. Realizing DL’s transformative potential requires interdisciplinary collaboration focused on standardized evaluation frameworks, diverse multi-institutional datasets, adaptive regulatory pathways for continuously learning algorithms, and ethical safeguards for privacy and equity. This structured narrative review serves as a practical guide for clinicians and engineers navigating the translation from algorithmic innovation to safe, equitable clinical adoption.

title: Unsupervised state-learning for multivariate time series data: a survey and practical guidelines
abstract: Abstract Unsupervised state-learning aims to infer latent variables or representations from multivariate time series that can serve as predictive summaries of a system evolution. Depending on the modelling assumptions, these summaries may appear as discrete regimes, posterior belief states, continuous latent trajectories or learnt embeddings that are subsequently interpreted or regularised as states. State-learning enables segmentation, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance and clinical monitoring, but the literature is fragmented across probabilistic regime-switching models, clustering and change-point methods, as well as modern representation learning. This survey unifies these strands and provides a synthesis aimed at practical method selection. We formalise the notion of state and introduce a taxonomy that makes modelling choices explicit along key dimensions: discrete versus continuous states, observable versus latent representations, output formats (hard assignments, posteriors, embeddings) and fixed versus adaptive state cardinality. We then review three major methodological families: probabilistic models, clustering/segmentation approaches, as well as self-supervised or generative representation learning. We highlight core assumptions, computational trade-offs and failure modes under missingness, irregular sampling, non-stationarity, as well as scarce evaluation labels. Building on this synthesis, we present a method-selection framework and implementation-oriented workflows that summarise recurring patterns in the literature and our practical reading of them, covering preprocessing, model fitting, diagnostics and uncertainty handling. Furthermore, we propose an evaluation and reporting protocol tailored to state-learning, emphasising leakage-free temporal splits, temporal coherence, interpretability, complexity control and uncertainty calibration. Finally, we summarise widely used benchmark testbeds that provide evaluation-only labels.

title: Partial differential equations in the age of machine learning: a critical synthesis of classical, machine learning, and hybrid methods
abstract: Abstract Partial differential equations (PDEs) govern physical phenomena across the full range of scientific scales, yet their computational solution remains one of the defining challenges of modern science. This critical review examines two mature but epistemologically distinct paradigms for PDE solution, classical numerical methods and machine learning approaches, through a unified evaluative framework structured around six fundamental computational challenges: high dimensionality, nonlinearity, geometric complexity, discontinuities, multiscale phenomena, and multiphysics coupling. Classical methods, including finite difference, finite element, finite volume, and spectral discretizations, are assessed for their structure-preserving properties, rigorous convergence theory, and scalable solver design; their persistent limitations in high-dimensional and geometrically complex settings are characterized in detail. Machine learning approaches, including physics-informed neural networks, neural operators, graph architectures, transformers, generative models, and hybrid frameworks, are evaluated under a taxonomy organized by the degree to which physical knowledge is incorporated, and subjected to the same critical assessment applied to classical methods. The central finding is that classical methods are deductive: errors are bounded by quantities derivable from PDE structure and discretization parameters. Machine learning methods are inductive: accuracy depends on statistical proximity to the training distribution. This distinction determines not which paradigm is superior, but what each can certify, and therefore where each should be deployed. Epistemological character, rather than computational speed, is the primary criterion governing responsible method selection. We identify three genuine complementarities between the paradigms and develop principles for hybrid design, including a framework for the structure inheritance problem and an error budget decomposition that separates discretization, neural approximation, and coupling contributions. We further assess emerging frontiers, including foundation models for scientific computing, differentiable programming for inverse design, quantum algorithms, and exascale co-design, evaluating each against the structural constraints that determine whether current barriers are fundamental or contingent on engineering progress. The conclusion is not that one paradigm supersedes the other, but that their principled integration, grounded in the complementary strengths each provides, offers the most credible path toward computationally tractable solutions to the most consequential open problems that neither can address alone.

title: Out-of-distribution challenges in intelligent fault diagnosis: a survey of generalization and detection
abstract: Deep learning (DL)-based intelligent fault diagnosis (IFD) has achieved strong performance in mechanical systems, but its reliability can deteriorate when deployment data differ from the training distribution because of changes in operating conditions, equipment, sensing environments, or fault semantics. These shifts create two related but distinct requirements: preserving accurate predictions for known fault categories under unseen yet relevant conditions and identifying inputs that should not be assigned to any known category. To support this survey, we conducted a reproducible search of IEEE Xplore, the Web of Science Core Collection, and Scopus for studies published from January 1, 2020, to July 16, 2026. The search returned 280 database records, of which 181 remained after deduplication and 161 primary mechanical OOD-related studies were included and coded according to their deployment roles and shift types. The survey focuses on the operational boundaries between generalization-oriented methods and detection-oriented methods in mechanical fault diagnosis. It does not aim to provide an exhaustive review of closed-set domain adaptation or domain generalization without an unseen mechanical-domain evaluation, general anomaly detection unrelated to unknown-fault rejection, non-mechanical industrial process monitoring, or general-purpose computer-vision OOD methods except where they provide necessary conceptual foundations. We introduce a task-relative operational definition based on effective training support, training label space, and a declared deployment envelope, and use it to distinguish condition-related (C-shift), fault-semantic (F-shift), and combined C+F settings. Based on these distinctions, we organize representative methods by deployment role and mechanism, compare their assumptions, data requirements, outputs, strengths, and limitations, and synthesize literature-reported experimental and evaluation practices. The resulting deployment-oriented perspective emphasizes that reliable diagnosis requires known-class generalization, calibrated OOD detection, and an explicit escalation or human-referral pathway to be evaluated separately and integrated coherently.

title: Towards efficient large language models for scientific data: a review
abstract: Abstract The adaptation of large language models (LLMs) to scientific domains requires efficient strategies to mitigate high computational costs while preserving performance. We present a systematic survey of efficiency techniques for adapting LLMs to scientific applications. Our review analyzes 120 studies across seven scientific fields, including biomedicine, clinical medicine, biology, mathematics, chemistry, geo-environmental science, and cross-domain scientific research. Across the surveyed literature, we summarize 34 representative models and 30 scientific datasets for efficient scientific LLM research. Examining parameter-efficient fine-tuning, knowledge distillation, architectural optimization, and data-centric approaches, we introduce a dual-axis taxonomy that organizes efficiency techniques by both methodological strategy and scientific domain. We further provide practical guidance for selecting efficiency strategies under resource constraints and highlight open challenges including multimodal integration, catastrophic forgetting, and automated method selection. By synthesizing cross-domain evidence and outlining directions for sustainable model development, this survey supports the adoption of efficient scientific LLMs in resource-constrained research environments and promotes more accessible and responsible deployment across scientific disciplines.

title: Toward robust, reproducible, and widely accessible intracranial speech brain-computer interfaces: a comprehensive narrative review of neural mechanisms, hardware, algorithms, evaluation, clinical pathways and future directions
abstract: Intracranial speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a promising route for restoring communication in individuals with severe, chronic, and otherwise irreversible motor and speech impairments who cannot communicate adequately using conventional assistive technologies, but clinical translation remains limited by fragmented and heterogeneous evidence, as well as unresolved design trade-offs across neuroscience, hardware, algorithms, validation methods, and clinical integration. This narrative review synthesizes recent progress across four key domains in intracranial speech neuroprosthetics: i) the neural mechanisms underlying overt, attempted (including silent miming and attempts without observable movement), and imagined speech (speech imagery without an attempt to articulate); ii) decision-oriented hardware comparisons of surgically implanted recording modalities, including microelectrode array (MEA), electrocorticography (ECoG), and stereotactic electroencephalography (SEEG); iii) experimental strategies for cross-subject generalization; and iv) advances in neural decoding, including sequence models, attention-based architectures (e.g., transformers), articulatory intermediate representations, and language-prior-assisted frameworks. We highlight persistent bottlenecks, including limited transfer without individual calibration, long-term non-stationarity and recalibration burden, heterogeneous and non-comparable evaluation practices, limited naturalistic expressivity, and the variable signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and limited temporal alignment of neural activity in imagined speech decoding. Our contributions are threefold: (1) an end-to-end, decision-oriented synthesis that links neural representations to recording choices, experimental design, decoding model architectures, and translational constraints; (2) a structured framework organized around five coupled design questions, accompanied by a unified evaluation framework and a conceptual cross-linguistic, cross-task benchmark template that integrates objective, perceptual, expressive, conversational, and longitudinal metrics; and (3) user-centered translational guidance that includes agency-preserving shared control, verifiable performance priorities, and scenario-specific minimum viable product (MVP) profiles for differentiating between reliability-first home communication and fidelity-first conversational speech restoration. We conclude with a call for larger multilingual, multi-center longitudinal datasets; harmonized benchmarks; adaptive yet interpretable decoders; prospective clinical validation; and transparent data-sharing and reporting practices with robust ethical safeguards. These efforts are essential to accelerate the safe and equitable deployment of speech neuroprostheses.

title: Beyond the survey: a systematic empirical study of detection and association in visual MOT
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive experimental evaluation and detailed analysis of state-of-the-art multi-object tracking algorithms, with an emphasis on quantifying the individual contributions of detection and association components to overall tracking performance. Unlike existing surveys that primarily offer theoretical categorizations or taxonomies of tracking methods, our work adopts a rigorous experimental perspective grounded in publicly available implementations, providing practical guidance for researchers and practitioners in method selection and system design. We introduce a unified pipeline diagram that consolidates the core components across the two main branches of visual multi-object tracking: tracking-by-detection and end-to-end deep learning paradigms, and systematically analyze the object detection, feature extraction, and data association modules. Through extensive empirical studies on standard benchmarks, including MOT16, MOT17, MOT20, SportsMOT, DanceTrack, and CrowdTrack datasets, we reveal critical insights: (1) detection quality dominates association strategy performance, with detector improvements yielding more than 10% gains compared to less than 5% from refined association strategies; (2) modern deep learning detectors paired with specialized re-identification models significantly outperform joint detection and embedding approaches; and (3) transformer-based end-to-end methods exhibit greater robustness to detection quality variations but at a substantial computational cost. Our findings from extensive experiments provide key insights into component-level effects in MOT, particularly the dominant influence of detection quality relative to association, while offering practical insights for designing and optimizing MOT systems under varying performance and robustness requirements.

title: Neuro-native paradigms of brain foundation models: evolution, taxonomy, and perspectives
abstract: The deep integration of artificial intelligence and neuroscience has catalyzed the development of brain foundation models designed to extract transferable neural representations from vast and unlabeled neurophysiological datasets. Initial first-generation models largely relied on isomorphic transfer by migrating architectures from large language models and vision transformers to the neural signal domain. Although these approaches demonstrated the value of scale, evidence across the literature also reveals recurring mismatches between general-purpose architectural assumptions and the spatial, temporal, and acquisition properties of neurophysiological recordings. Yet the field lacks a unified account of how models have moved from general-purpose architectural transfer to designs that explicitly encode neurophysiological structure, and why this transition matters for cross-subject and cross-device generalization. This review addresses this need by tracing the evolution from 2021 to 2025 of EEG-centered neuroelectrophysiological foundation models from isomorphic adaptation toward second-generation neuro-native architectures. Unlike simple parameter expansion, these next-generation architectures are characterized by the explicit incorporation of neuro-inductive biases. We organize these models into four core neuro-native paradigms based on their design principles, encompassing topology awareness using coordinate manifold mapping, brain-like efficiency employing linear state space models, multi-scale hierarchy mirroring recursive organization, and semantic fusion bridging the neuro-semantic gap. Taken together, these developments suggest that neurophysiological priors can improve transfer and computational efficiency when they match the task and acquisition setting. Their broader clinical and causal value remains to be established through controlled, cross-subject, cross-device, and intervention-aware validation.

title: A systematic survey of open-ended visual segmentation: taxonomies, challenges and future directions
abstract: Visual segmentation is a cornerstone of computer vision, enabling pixel-level scene understanding for critical applications such as autonomous driving and medical imaging. However, traditional visual models operating under the closed-world assumption struggle with dynamic environment changes and emerging unknown objects. To overcome these limitations, research has shifted toward open-ended environments, categorizing into three distinct research directions: Open-Set Segmentation (OSS), Open-Vocabulary Segmentation (OVS), and Open-World Segmentation (OWS). To provide an informative introduction to researchers who are new to this topic, our paper provides a systematic and comprehensive survey on the development of Open-Ended Visual Segmentation. First, a unified reference framework is established for these research categories, while common datasets and evaluation metrics are summarized. Subsequently, existing methodologies are categorized according to their technical hierarchies: OSS focuses on the binary discrimination of unknown classes; OVS leverages large-scale Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for zero-shot generalization via natural language prompts; and OWS emphasizes autonomous discovery and incremental knowledge maintenance. Moreover, key methodological routes are systematically classified. In particular, it covers the uncertainty estimation, vision-language alignment, and knowledge distillation. Meanwhile, this work also provides an in-depth analysis and quantitative performance comparisons of state-of-the-art techniques in these domains. Finally, prevalent challenges including computational efficiency, semantic ambiguity, and the lack of unified benchmarks are discussed, with potential research trajectories outlined to provide an informative survey and a valuable resource to researchers for subsequent technological developments and innovation. The collected methods and datasets will be made publicly available at https://github.com/CVLife/Awesome-Open-ended-Segmentation .

title: Deep learning for real-time strawberry detection, ripeness classification, and picking point localization: a review of architectures, field studies, and open challenges
abstract: Abstract Accurate detection of strawberry fruit, reliable ripeness estimation, and precise localization of the picking point are essential for automated harvesting and yield prediction in smart farming. However, real-world environments introduce significant challenges, including occlusion, illumination variability, and high visual similarity between ripeness stages. Deep learning (DL)-based object detection methods have become the dominant approach to address these issues. This paper presents a systematic review of 60 peer-reviewed studies published between 2023 and 2026, focusing on detecting strawberries and their ripeness using the YOLO family (v5–v11) of DL algorithms. The studies are analyzed with respect to dataset characteristics, preprocessing and augmentation strategies, model architectures, and evaluation protocols. Our results show a clear dominance of YOLOv8 (28 studies, 46.7%) and YOLOv11 (13 studies, 21.7%), while hybrid CNN–ViT models are gaining attention (8 studies, 13.3%). However, critical methodological issues are identified: in 21 out of 60 studies (35.0%), data augmentation was applied before dataset splitting, 13 studies (21.7%) adhered to the recommended split-then-augment protocol, and 8 studies (13.3%) applied online augmentation. The remaining 18 studies (30.0%) did not report using any augmentation. Reproducibility is severely limited by scarce sharing of code or trained weights (2 studies, 3.3%) and datasets (8 studies, 13.3%). To quantify the empirical impact of this methodological flaw, we conducted a controlled experiment on the StrawDI_Db1 dataset using YOLOv8, comparing four augmentation strategies. The results demonstrate that the full leakage protocol overestimates test performance by 11.76 to 19.28 percentage points (p.p.) in mAP@0.5:0.95 (and by 8.02 to 11.50 p.p. in mAP@0.50) compared to a clean, split-then-augment pipeline. The underlying validation-test discrepancy reaches up to 18.63 p.p. (mAP@0.5:0.95) and 13.81 p.p. (mAP@0.50). These findings provide direct quantitative evidence that the performance metrics reported in 35.0% of the reviewed studies may be substantially inflated. This review provides a structured overview of current approaches, a critical assessment of existing research practices, and actionable guidance for developing robust, deployment-ready DL solutions for precision agriculture.

title: From prototype to deployment: a systematic review of real-time YOLO-based deep learning methods for railway track defect detection
abstract: Railway infrastructure safety relies on the timely detection of track defects, the failure of which can result in severe operational disruptions and accidents. Recent advances in deep learning and computer vision, particularly YOLO-based object detection, have produced encouraging solutions for in-service railway inspection. Yet substantial inconsistencies persist in how real-time performance is defined, evaluated, and translated into deployable systems. This study presents a systematic literature review of YOLO-based railway track defect detection methods published between 2020 and 2026, conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. From 131 records retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus, 44 studies were retained after rigorous screening. The review is structured around seven research questions covering computer vision tasks, real-time detection capability, model architectures, system limitations, computational platforms, dataset and metric standardization, and deployment feasibility. Within the reviewed corpus, object detection was the most frequent task (72.7% as a standalone task), with YOLO-based architectures serving as the proposed primary method in roughly 89% of studies—a composition that, by the review’s YOLO-focused design, characterizes this subset rather than the prevalence of YOLO across railway inspection at large. Although the entire corpus is framed around real-time operation, an explicit speed-and-hardware rule classified only 63.6% of studies as offering high real-time feasibility, and reported throughput varied considerably (from below 1 to about 279 FPS) across heterogeneous hardware, reflecting the absence of standardized evaluation criteria. Although most studies motivate their designs by onboard or edge deployment, only 7 (15.9%) measure inference on edge/embedded hardware or on board a vehicle, and only 2 run their systems on track. Despite frequently reported accuracies exceeding 90% mAP, no study demonstrates fully operational, system-level deployment: coded against a TRL-based rubric, all 44 studies remain at levels L1–L3, and 84.1% do not progress beyond offline evaluation (L1–L2), revealing a marked gap between experimental performance and operational readiness. The review further identifies recurring challenges in dataset diversity, class imbalance, real-world validation, and metric reporting. Four contributions are made: (i) a PRISMA-compliant synthesis of recent YOLO-based literature, (ii) a systematic account of how the term “real-time” is operationally underspecified, (iii) an evidence-based quantification of the deployment maturity gap, and (iv) recommendations for methodological standardization. Bridging the divide between algorithmic performance and operational deployment remains the central challenge for next-generation intelligent railway inspection systems.

title: Building the trust: AI-based systematic literature review of deepfake detection across modalities and domains
abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) based generative models have advanced rapidly, making it possible to generate highly realistic synthetic media. These technologies build new opportunities for creative and legitimate use in various domains, but they also give rise to significant concerns about digital trust and privacy. Though it has various legitimate uses, it can also be used to generate harmful content, often known as "deepfake". It can cause political misinformation, non-consensual content generation and financial fraud that costs millions. These consequences are harmful for democracy, healthcare and the legal system. One of the growing concerns is the emergence of deepfake in medical imaging, where fabrication and manipulation of diagnostic scans and clinical imagery directly threaten patient safety, healthcare integrity and medical forensics. This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of various deepfake generation and detection methods based on Artificial intelligence. Following the PRISMA framework , relevant studies are identified from major scientific databases, including IEEE Xplore, Scopus, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Google scholar and ACM Digital Library. Following a PRISMA-based search and screening process, 142 primary studies were selected from an initial pool of studies, based on predefined inclusion, exclusion, and quality-assessment criteria. Some literature published prior to 2021 is additionally cited for contextual background, separate from the 142 primary studies reviewed. The selected literature is analysed and categorised into different deepfake generation and detection methods. Furthermore, benchmark datasets, evaluation protocols and comparative performance trends are analysed. Key challenges such as dataset bias, poor generalization, adversarial vulnerability and lack of explainability are discussed. Future research directions are outlined. This review aims to serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners working on reliable deepfake detection systems.

title: Artificial intelligence for water quality monitoring: a PRISMA-based systematic literature review, taxonomy, comparative analysis, and future research directions
abstract: Abstract Accurate and reliable water quality monitoring (WQM) has become increasingly important due to rapid urbanization, industrialization, climate change, and anthropogenic activities that threaten global freshwater resources. Conventional water quality assessment methods primarily rely on manual sampling and laboratory analysis, which are labour-intensive, time-consuming, costly, and unsuitable for continuous real-time monitoring of large-scale aquatic environments. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and sensing technologies have enabled intelligent, data-driven approaches capable of modelling complex nonlinear relationships, detecting contamination events, and improving predictive decision-making. This study presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of AI-based water quality monitoring using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework. A systematic search of IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink identified studies published between 2020 and 2026, of which 91 met the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Review and survey articles were excluded from the analytical corpus so that secondary literature was not pooled with primary studies. A structured taxonomy is developed to characterise the strengths, limitations, interpretability and reported applicability of these model families. Because the included studies differ in target variable, dataset, preprocessing and validation protocol, no pooled performance comparison across model categories is reported and no meta-analysis was undertaken. The review identifies key challenges, including heterogeneous datasets, limited model generalization, overfitting, computational complexity, sensor calibration issues, data inconsistency, and the lack of standardized benchmark datasets. Furthermore, emerging research directions comprising Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), Federated Learning, Edge AI, Graph Neural Networks, Digital Twins, Foundation Models, and multimodal environmental intelligence are discussed. The findings provide researchers, practitioners and policymakers with a structured reference to the current evidence base on AI-based water quality monitoring, together with the methodological limitations of that evidence, to inform the development of future monitoring systems for sustainable water resource management.

title: The landscape of computer vision datasets in smart agriculture: trends, taxonomies, challenges, and future directions
abstract: Abstract Modern agriculture is increasingly driven by data-centric and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled approaches to improve productivity, resource efficiency, and precision in decision-making. In this context, computer vision datasets have emerged as critical resources for enabling automated agricultural analysis. This study presents a large-scale, data-centric review of agricultural computer vision datasets using a PRISMA-guided systematic review methodology. A systematic search of the peer-reviewed data journals Scientific Data and Data in Brief, conducted through 31 January 2026, identified 2,308 records, from which 253 eligible dataset publications were retained after duplicate removal and eligibility screening based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. We systematically analyze the dataset landscape across multiple dimensions, including vision tasks, annotation strategies, acquisition environments, sensing modalities, and geographic distribution. Furthermore, we propose a unified multi-dimensional taxonomy that organizes datasets based on task orientation, semantic content, and design characteristics, enabling structured comparison and informed dataset selection. Our analysis identifies key limitations, including sampling bias, underrepresentation of crops and regions, inconsistent annotation practices, and limited interoperability, which collectively hinder reproducibility and model generalization. Additionally, challenges in dataset accessibility and the absence of standardized benchmarking frameworks restrict effective knowledge transfer. Finally, we outline critical directions for future research, emphasizing standardized dataset design, scalable annotation frameworks, and robust evaluation protocols to support the development of reliable and generalizable agricultural AI systems.
